title: How to schedule social media posts in advance on Mac for realtors in 2026
metaTitle: Schedule Social Media Posts in Advance on Mac for Realtors
description: Schedule social media posts in advance on your Mac with one weekly batch, a content sheet and a free scheduler tier. Realtor steps, costs and fixes.
targetKeyword: schedule social media posts in advance
secondaryKeywords: real estate social media batch posting
intro: To schedule social media posts in advance on your Mac, pick one scheduler, write a week of captions in one sitting, and set each post's date and time. Daily posting then becomes one planned session a week. This page shows what slow posting costs, why it keeps happening, and the fixes you can use without buying anything.
tldr: Batch one week of captions and photos in a single sitting, then queue the posts.
Keep one content sheet in Google Sheets as the record of dates, copy and status.
Set up Text Replacements in System Settings > Keyboard > Text Replacements for the parts you type every week.
Build the compliance line into every template, and confirm the wording with your broker.
Ask Lazur for draft captions and click by click help. You still review and post.

blocks.text: What slow posting costs a realtor

Most of the cost is time, and almost nobody measures it. We found no public study that times how long agents spend on posts, so this page cannot give you an hour count. You can still measure your own week. Time one post from the first idea to the last click. Then multiply that time by the number of posts you publish each week. Seeing the total makes the cost easy to judge.

Pay is the second part. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reports a May 2025 median of $52,830 a year for real estate sales agents. It also reports that 54% of sales agents are self-employed. If you are one of them, nobody pays you for the hours you spend on posts. Those hours come out of the same week you use for showings, calls and paperwork.

The time cost is also about where your attention goes. The 2026 NAR Member Profile, as reported by HousingWire, says 62% of Realtors got none of their 2025 business from in-person open houses. Median shares were 28% from repeat clients and 22% from past-client referrals. Those relationships deserve time too. A post routine that eats the hour you would spend calling past clients is a bad trade.
Where the minutes go in a typical posting session
A single post looks simple. In practice it has six or seven small steps, and each one invites a distraction. Here is where most agents lose time, roughly in the order it happens.

items: Finding a photo across your phone, camera roll and listing folder.
Rewriting the same listing details for each platform.
Checking price, address and open house time against the listing sheet.
Cropping or resizing the image for each platform.
Switching accounts and hunting for the post button.
Waiting for a broker or team member to approve the wording.

blocks.text: Scheduling does not remove these steps. It moves them. Batching moves most of them into one session, so you do the hunt, the check and the resize once for a whole week instead of seven times.
Which scheduler fits a Mac

Start with one question. Which platforms do your buyers and sellers actually use? For many realtors that means Facebook and Instagram. The table compares three paid scheduling tools and one browser tool. The prices come from each vendor's pricing page as of 2026-11-07. Check the page again before you buy, because plans change.

blocks.text: Buffer's free plan is the cheapest way to test a routine. It covers up to 3 channels and 10 scheduled posts on each channel. That is enough to run a weekly batch on two platforms before you pay anything. The same page says channels above 10 cost less per channel, which matters only if you run a large account.

Later and Hootsuite cost more and have no free plan. Both offer a 14-day trial, so you can test them before you commit. Hootsuite's Standard plan manages up to 10 social accounts. If you run one main account and one team account, you will likely need far less than that.

Meta Business Suite runs in a browser on your Mac and covers Facebook and Instagram. Online guides disagree on how far ahead you can schedule. Check Meta's Business Help Center before you plan more than a few weeks ahead, and trust the help center over a blog post.

Canva is the design step, not the scheduler. Canva's help page did not open during our research, so we cannot confirm what its scheduling options include. Look at Canva's own help center before you plan a queue around it.
Set up your Mac so captions take seconds

Text Replacements turn a short code into a full block of text. Use it for your sign-off, your brokerage line, a standard hashtag set and a link to your site. You set it once. After that it works in most apps that accept typed text, so the repeat typing stops.

items: Open System Settings, then choose Keyboard.
Click Add. Enter the short text, then the full replacement.
Click Add and Done. Type your short text in any app to test it.

blocks.text: The Shortcuts app is useful for opening things. Build a shortcut that opens your content sheet and your scheduler in one run. Apple's Shortcuts guide describes multi-step shortcuts and includes a Gallery of examples. The guide does not confirm that shortcuts run on a timer, so treat Shortcuts as a launcher, not a poster.
Write captions in batches without sounding like a form letter

A batch works best with a fixed pattern. Use one line that catches attention, one fact from the listing, one next step and your sign-off. Keep the pattern the same across posts, but change the words. Here is a sample for a new listing: 'New on Cedar Lane. Fenced yard, bright kitchen, open house Saturday morning. Message me for the floor plan.' The sample is made up, so swap in your own details.

AI can write the first draft. NAR's 2026 Technology Report says about 56% of REALTORS use AI to create social media posts. Give the tool the listing sheet, ask for three short versions, and pick the best one. Then check every price, address, date and feature against the source. Never let a draft introduce a detail you did not give it.
Compliance rules to build into every post

Compliance is the part many agents skip when they rush. Florida Realtors, summarizing NAR guidance on September 30, 2025, says brokerages should require all posts to follow advertising, fair housing and antitrust rules. It also says to specify required ad details, such as the brokerage name and license number. It recommends reviewing the social media policy at least once a year.

blocks.title: Check your broker first
blocks.text: Your brokerage and state rules decide what belongs in an ad. Put the required wording in your caption template once, then reuse it. Follow your employer's rules on client data too, including buyer names, addresses and contact details.

Build the check into the template instead of into each post. Add the brokerage line and license field to the bottom of every template. When a post goes into the content sheet, mark it reviewed with the date. A reviewed status column makes it hard to queue something nobody has checked.
Mistakes that cancel out the time you saved

items: Queueing a post for a listing that went under contract the same week.
Copying one caption to every platform without changing the length or tone.
Scheduling a month of posts, then never checking the queue again.
Leaving comments unanswered because the post felt automatic.
Keeping photos in three folders, so the right one is always missing.
Skipping the compliance line to save a few minutes.

blocks.text: Most of these mistakes cost more time than they save. Fix them with a status column, a short weekly review and one photo folder per listing. None of those fixes need a new app.

Some posts age fast. A market update or a rate comment can go stale in days. Queue evergreen posts, such as a neighborhood guide or a buyer tip, a few weeks ahead. Keep time-sensitive posts for the week they apply, and write them in the batch that day.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Hold fn to dictate clean text at the cursor in any app. Lazur does not click buttons, post for you, or schedule posts. You still choose the date and press the button.

The most useful help is drafting. Say the listing details out loud, ask for three caption drafts in your tone, and read them back. Then change the wording and paste the one you keep. Lazur drafts and types text. You check it before it goes anywhere.

When you cannot find a control, ask where it is. Lazur draws a circle and a label around the option on your screen. If you want steps, ask Lazur to walk you through it. It guides you one click at a time and waits for each click.

Lazur can also set reminders in Apple Reminders by voice. Ask it to remind you to check the queue on Thursday. For comparing plans, Lazur can run a research job in its own Chrome tabs and return a summary and a report. Check any price on the vendor's pricing page before you pay.
Start small, then grow the queue

Begin with the two platforms where your clients already spend time. Run a weekly batch for four weeks. Count how many posts you published, how many you skipped and how many took longer than planned. Add a third channel only after the first two run for a full month without skipped weeks.
What to do next

Pick one scheduler and one content sheet this week. Set up the Text Replacements and the compliance line. Batch your next week of posts in one sitting, then check the queue on the day you planned. The first batch is the slowest. The second one goes faster, because the setup is already done.

faq.question: Can I schedule social media posts in advance from a Mac without a paid app?
faq.answer: Yes, for some platforms. Meta Business Suite runs in a browser on your Mac and covers Facebook and Instagram. Check Meta's Business Help Center for current scheduling limits, because online guides disagree on them.

faq.question: Is Buffer's free plan enough for a realtor?
faq.answer: It connects up to 3 channels and allows 10 scheduled posts per channel. That is enough to test a weekly routine on two platforms. Check buffer.com for current limits before you rely on it.

faq.question: How far ahead should I schedule posts?
faq.answer: Schedule evergreen posts a few weeks ahead. Keep time-sensitive posts for the week they apply. Check your platform's help center for its scheduling window, because sources disagree on the exact limit.

faq.question: Do I need to tell my broker about scheduled posts?
faq.answer: Ask your brokerage what it requires. Florida Realtors, summarizing NAR guidance, says brokerages should require posts to follow advertising, fair housing and antitrust rules. Your state and brokerage may have their own rules.

faq.question: Can Lazur schedule posts for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons or operate other apps. It drafts text, points at the schedule button and guides you one click at a time. You choose the date and press the button yourself.

faq.question: Is it safe to use AI to write my captions?
faq.answer: Use it for a first draft, then check every price, address, date and feature against your listing sheet. NAR's 2026 Technology Report says about 56% of REALTORS use AI to create social posts, so many agents already do this.

faq.question: What if a listing sells after I scheduled posts about it?
faq.answer: Pull or edit the queued posts as soon as the status changes. Keep a listing status column in your content sheet, and check it on your weekly review day.

faq.question: Does a posting routine matter if most of my business comes from referrals?
faq.answer: It can help, but keep the goal in view. HousingWire's report on the 2026 NAR Member Profile shows median shares of 28% from repeat clients and 22% from past-client referrals. Posts can support those relationships, but they do not replace direct calls.

faq.question: Do I need Canva to schedule social media posts?
faq.answer: No. Canva is useful for design work. Its help page did not open during our research, so confirm its scheduling options in Canva directly before you plan around them.

costs.title: Unpaid hours from a self-employed job
costs.text: The Bureau of Labor Statistics reports that 54% of real estate sales agents are self-employed. Posting time is not billed, paid or tracked by an employer. It comes out of the week you could spend on showings, calls or past-client follow-up.

costs.title: Posting that goes quiet
costs.text: HousingWire's summary of the 2026 NAR Member Profile says 55% of Realtors use social media apps daily or nearly daily for business. Your clients see your account only when you post. A quiet feed wastes attention you already paid to earn.

costs.title: Time taken from relationships
costs.text: HousingWire's summary of the 2026 NAR Member Profile says a median 28% of business came from repeat clients and 22% from past-client referrals. Time spent on posts can crowd out the calls that feed those numbers.

costs.title: Compliance mistakes
costs.text: A post that breaks advertising or fair housing rules can cost more than the hours you saved. Florida Realtors, summarizing NAR guidance, says brokerages should require posts to follow those rules. The exact risk depends on your brokerage and state, so ask your broker.

costs.title: Tool spending that adds up
costs.text: Hootsuite's Standard plan lists $99 per user per month on annual billing. Later's Starter plan lists $18.75 per month, billed yearly. Buffer lists $5 per channel per month. Pick a tool by the platforms you use, not by its longest feature list.

causes.title: Every post starts from a blank page
causes.text: Most realtors write each caption fresh. The listing details live in one place, the caption idea in another and the photo somewhere else. Each time, you rebuild the post from scratch. A template with fixed slots removes that step.

causes.title: Each platform wants its own version
causes.text: A post for Facebook, Instagram and a neighborhood group may need different sizes, lengths and hashtags. You resize, rewrite and log in separately for each one. That repeat work adds up fast for one single message.

causes.title: There is no content calendar
causes.text: Without a calendar, you decide what to post each morning. That means a new decision, a new search for a photo and a new caption. A content sheet with dates, channels and status turns those decisions into one planned review.

causes.title: Posting waits for a free hour
causes.text: When posting depends on a free hour, it happens after a closing or between showings. Posts go up late, or not at all. Irregular posting also makes the work feel bigger, because you face a backlog before you start.

causes.title: Approval happens too late
causes.text: If the broker check comes at the very end, a finished post can sit for days. Then it gets edited, reapproved and rescheduled. Put the compliance line in the template, so most posts pass on the first review.

causes.title: Photos live in too many places
causes.text: Listing photos sit in the MLS, the camera roll, a shared drive and a text thread. Finding the right image eats minutes before you write a word. One photo folder per listing removes most of that hunt.

fixes.title: Batch one week in one sitting
fixes.text: Pick the same time each week, such as a Monday morning before your first showing. Draft, check and queue the week's posts in one run. Batching removes the repeated setup, the photo hunt and the login switching.

fixes.title: Build a content sheet in Google Sheets
fixes.text: Make one sheet with these columns: date, channel, listing or topic, photo link, caption, compliance check and status. Press ⌘ L in Chrome to jump to the sheet. Change the status to queued once a post is scheduled, so nothing goes out twice.

fixes.title: Start with one scheduler and two channels
fixes.text: Buffer's free plan covers up to 3 channels and 10 scheduled posts per channel. Meta Business Suite runs in a browser for Facebook and Instagram. Pick the one that matches your channels, and test it for a month before you pay for anything.

fixes.title: Set up Text Replacements for repeat text
fixes.text: Open System Settings > Keyboard > Text Replacements. Add short codes for your sign-off, brokerage line, standard hashtags and website link. Typing the code drops in the full text. This takes minutes once and saves the same typing every week.

fixes.title: Keep a short template library
fixes.text: Write one template for each common post type, such as new listing, open house, price change, sold and buyer tip. Each template has fixed slots for address, price, photo and next step. Store them in the content sheet or in a Notes document.

fixes.title: Draft with AI, then verify against the listing
fixes.text: Give an AI tool the listing sheet and ask for a short draft. Check each price, date and feature against the source before it goes into the queue. NAR's 2026 Technology Report says about 56% of REALTORS use AI for social posts, so the habit is common.

fixes.title: Put the compliance line in the template
fixes.text: Add the brokerage name, the license field and any ad line your brokerage requires to every template. Ask your broker to approve the template once. Florida Realtors recommends reviewing the social media policy at least once a year, so ask when it was last reviewed.

fixes.title: Use Gmail's scheduled send for email updates
fixes.text: To reach past clients by email, Gmail's scheduled send works for that channel. Compose the update, click the arrow next to Send, then choose Schedule send. Keep email on its own schedule, separate from your social calendar.

fixes.title: Check the queue once a day
fixes.text: Set a short daily check to answer comments and see what is queued next. Scheduled posts still need replies. If a listing changes status, pull the post before it goes out.

plan.label: Monday
plan.title: Pick your tools
plan.text: Choose one scheduler and the two channels your clients use. Create the content sheet with date, channel, photo, caption, compliance and status columns. Add Text Replacements for your sign-off and brokerage line.

plan.label: Tuesday
plan.title: Gather photos
plan.text: Create one folder per active listing and one for evergreen images. Rename files with the address. Move the best photo for each post into its folder, so the hunt takes seconds next time.

plan.label: Wednesday
plan.title: Draft the batch
plan.text: Write the week's captions from your templates. Ask Lazur for two or three alternate lines on the hardest posts. Read each draft aloud, then check every fact against the listing sheet.

plan.label: Thursday
plan.title: Queue and check
plan.text: Schedule each post in your chosen tool. Preview it on your phone too. Mark each row as queued in the content sheet, and add the date the broker reviewed it.

plan.label: Friday
plan.title: Review and reply
plan.text: Check the queue, answer comments and note which posts drew the most replies. Pull any post whose listing changed status. Write two changes for next week, then close the sheet.
